# Checking a model

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(rnetis)
```

rnetis reports quantities, not verdicts. Nothing here prints "good fit" or
"assumption satisfied". This vignette uses one fit on one network and one on
several.

```{r}
fit <- fit_influence(
  y ~ ar() + exposure(y, via = tie, normalize = "row"),
  data = demo_influence
)
mg <- fit_influence(
  y ~ ar() + exposure(x, via = tie) + (1 | group),
  data = demo_influence_groups
)
```

## List what the fit assumes

```{r}
netis_assumptions(fit)
```

Each row reports three things:

| Field | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| `source` | Is this maintained by the model, rnetis's default, or your declaration? |
| `handling` | Does anything in the fit address it? |
| `diagnostic_evidence` | `"not_testable"`, with the reason, where no statistic from a fit can bear on the row; otherwise `"none"`. |

Most rows read `unaddressed`. The dynamic-panel estimators that address sequential
exogeneity and persistent actor heterogeneity need more than the one transition a
fit analyzes, so none of the package's estimators has a device for them.

Two things about the design are yours to declare. A declaration changes what the
fit reports and no estimate:

```{r}
declared <- fit_influence(
  y ~ ar() + exposure(y, via = tie, normalize = "row"),
  data = demo_influence,
  network_exogeneity = "exogenous",
  exposure_orthogonal_to_actor_effect = TRUE
)
netis_assumptions(declared)$network$exogeneity
all.equal(coef(fit), coef(declared))
```

## Look at residual dependence

`netis_dependence()` needs the data as well as the fit, because it rebuilds the
network from the data.

```{r}
netis_dependence(fit, demo_influence)
```

The Moran-type statistic is reported without a reference distribution, because
the usual analytical moments are not derived for a directed `W`. It is not
confined to `[-1, 1]`. Within-unit serial correlation reads "not applicable",
since each actor has one outcome row.

With at least five networks the record also reports `residual_eta_squared`, the
between-group sum of squares of the residuals over the total. This eta-squared is
above zero in expectation with no group effect at all: `(J - 1) / (N - 1)` for `J`
groups and `N` rows, and larger when groups are small (Bliese & Halverson 1998).

## Compare standard errors

`influence_se_comparison()` sets the model's standard errors beside clustered
ones (Liang & Zeger 1986; Bell & McCaffrey 2002).

```{r message = FALSE}
influence_se_comparison(mg, by = "group")
attr(influence_se_comparison(mg, by = "group"), "addresses")
```

`by = "group"` clusters on the network. It permits arbitrary residual dependence
within each network and assumes independence between them, so it needs several
networks and is refused on one:

```{r error = TRUE}
influence_se_comparison(fit, by = "group")
```

`by = "node"` clusters on the actor. It is a different correction, is never
network-robust, and is refused on a mixed fit:

```{r}
attr(influence_se_comparison(fit, by = "node"), "addresses")
```

## Check agreement before aggregating

Where a construct is aggregated to the group, ask whether the group mean is
reliable. `icc1()` is the one-way ANOVA ICC(1) of Bliese (2000), on the rows the
fit used, and it differs from the conditional share in
`netis_variance_components()`. `icc2()` is the reliability of the group mean.

```{r}
icc1(mg)
icc2(mg)
```

For rater agreement on a scale, `rwg()` and `rwg_j()` implement James, Demaree &
Wolf (1984). `rwg()` takes one item and `rwg_j()` a matrix of items. The null
decides the answer, so it has no default.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
ratings <- matrix(stats::rnorm(60, 4, 0.4), ncol = 3)
teams <- rep(c("a", "b"), each = 10)
rwg(ratings[, 1], teams, null = list(dist = "uniform", n_options = 5))
rwg_j(ratings, teams, null = list(dist = "uniform", n_options = 5))
```

## What none of this establishes

No surface here tells you the model is right, or that an association is influence.
Homophilous selection on an unobserved trait produces the same pattern, and no
diagnostic here distinguishes them (`vignette("latent-space")`). Together these
tools tell you:

* what the fit takes for granted, and which of those nothing addresses;
* what the residuals look like with respect to the network and the groups, as
  numbers without a reference distribution;
* what a different variance assumption does to the standard errors;
* whether a group-level aggregate is reliable enough to model.

The step from "no adverse evidence" to "the assumption holds" is yours.

## References

Bell, R. M. and McCaffrey, D. F. (2002) Bias reduction in standard errors for
linear regression with multi-stage samples. *Survey Methodology* **28**(2), 169–181.

Bliese, P. D. (2000) Within-group agreement, non-independence, and reliability:
implications for data aggregation and analysis. In K. J. Klein and S. W. J.
Kozlowski (eds), *Multilevel Theory, Research, and Methods in Organizations*,
349–381. Jossey-Bass, San Francisco.

Bliese, P. D. and Halverson, R. R. (1998) Group size and measures of group-level
properties: an examination of eta-squared and ICC values. *Journal of Management*
**24**(2), 157–172.

James, L. R., Demaree, R. G. and Wolf, G. (1984) Estimating within-group
interrater reliability with and without response bias. *Journal of Applied
Psychology* **69**(1), 85–98.

Liang, K.-Y. and Zeger, S. L. (1986) Longitudinal data analysis using
generalized linear models. *Biometrika* **73**(1), 13–22.
